text: A song of ascents. Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in his ways.
You will eat the labor of your hands; blessed are you, and it will go well with you.

versions.text: You will eat the fruit of your labor; blessed are you, and it will go well with you.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew יְגִיעַ כַּפֶּיךָ literally means "the toil of your palms/hands." "Fruit of your labor" is a fair idiom but loses the concrete image of hands at work that gives the line its force; retaining "of your hands" is both more literal and equally natural for oral reading.

text: Your wife will be like a fruitful vine in the heart of your house; your children like young olive shoots around your table.

versions.text: Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children like young olive trees around your table.
versions.explanation: בְּיַרְכְּתֵי means "in the innermost recesses of," a stronger image than the general "within"; and שְׁתִלֵי זֵיתִים refers to olive shoots or saplings transplanted around the parent tree, which sharpens the picture of children gathered around the table.

text: Look! This is how the man is blessed who fears the LORD.

versions.text: So indeed is the man blessed who fears the LORD.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew opens with the attention-marker הִנֵּה ("behold/look"), which the current rendering drops, and the inverted word order ("So indeed is the man blessed") reads awkwardly aloud and separates "the man" from the relative clause "who fears the LORD." A clearer, more rhythmic ordering preserves the demonstrative force of כִי־כֵן ("thus, in this way").

text: May the LORD bless you from Zion; may you see the good of Jerusalem all the days of your life.
May you see your children's children. Peace be upon Israel!
